slides.title: What We're Covering Today
slides.intro: Until now we've written individual contracts — variables, arrays, mappings, structs, modifiers, constructors, events. Today we learn how real projects like OpenZeppelin and ERC20 organize code across multiple contracts.

slides.title: Topic 1 — What Is Inheritance?
slides.intro: An Animal has common features like eating and sleeping. A Dog is an Animal, so it automatically has those features. A German Shepherd is also a Dog, so it inherits everything Dog has too.
slides.note: Child contracts automatically receive everything their parent defines — no copy-pasting required.

slides.title: Example 1 — A Parent Contract
slides.intro: Animal defines one function. Deploy it and call eat() — it returns the string below.
slides.note: Now declare Dog is Animal with an empty body — deploy it, and Dog already has eat(). We didn't write the function again; Dog inherited it automatically.

slides.title: Example 2 — Adding a Second Parent Function
slides.intro: Add sleep() to Animal and redeploy. Dog now exposes both inherited functions without any extra code in Dog itself.
slides.note: sleep() returns "Animal is sleeping" — and Dog has it for free.

slides.title: Topic 2 — Parent Functions + Child Functions
slides.diagramNote: A child contract keeps every parent function AND can add its own. Both exist side by side.

slides.title: Topic 3 — Constructor Inheritance
slides.intro: When Dog is deployed, the parent constructor runs first, then the child constructor. Dog passes a fixed value up to Animal's constructor.
slides.note: Deploying Dog triggers Animal's constructor automatically — name is set before Dog's own constructor body runs.

slides.title: Topic 4 — Function Overloading
slides.intro: Same function name, different parameters. The compiler picks the right version based on the arguments you pass.
slides.note: Same idea appears constantly in real contracts: deposit(), deposit(uint amount), deposit(address user, uint amount).

slides.title: Topic 5 — Function Overriding
slides.diagramNote: Deploy Dog and call sound() — students see "Bark" returned instead of "Animal", proving the child version ran.

slides.title: Topic 1 — Enums: Fixed Sets of Values
slides.intro: Enums are used when values are limited — like a traffic light, which is only ever Red, Yellow, or Green (never Blue, Pink, or Orange).
slides.note: enum Status { Pending, Processing, Completed, Cancelled } — these are fixed, named values.

slides.title: Enum in Practice — An Order Contract
slides.intro: Status defaults to Pending. Each function moves the order forward one fixed step.
slides.note: Deploy, call ship() then deliver(), and read orderStatus after each step.

slides.title: Topic 2 — Abstract Contracts
slides.intro: An abstract contract is an incomplete contract — a blueprint, not a finished building. It cannot be deployed on its own.
slides.note: abstract contract Animal declares sound() with no body — just a signature. Only a child that implements it can be deployed.

slides.title: Abstract Contract — Declaration Without Body
slides.intro: The parent only declares the function signature. The child must supply the implementation before it can be deployed.
slides.note: Dog can be deployed. Animal cannot — it's missing a real implementation.

slides.title: Topic 3 — Interfaces
slides.intro: An interface is a contract agreement — like a TV remote. Every TV understands Power, Volume, and Channel, even though the manufacturer inside changes.
slides.note: The buttons (function signatures) stay the same; the implementation behind them can differ.

slides.title: Declaring and Implementing an Interface
slides.intro: An interface only lists function signatures. A contract that implements it must match those signatures exactly.
slides.note: Deploy Calculator directly and it works exactly like any normal contract.

slides.title: Topic 4 — Calling Another Contract Through an Interface
slides.intro: Deploy Calculator, then pass its address into a second contract that calls it through the interface — contracts talking to contracts.
slides.note: function calculate(address calculator) public view returns (uint) { return ICalculator(calculator).add(5, 3); }  →  returns 8

slides.title: Why Interfaces Matter
slides.intro: Almost every production protocol talks to other contracts through an interface rather than knowing their internal implementation:
